story_text: Leyra reached the Root Bridge with her breath coming fast and her thoughts running even faster. The bridge hung across the hollow like a giant's braid, thick roots twisted over thicker roots, silver-brown and mossy, swaying very slightly in the cool air. On the far side she could see the lanterns of the Commons glowing between the trunks. It looked so close. A dozen quick steps, maybe twenty, and she would be there. She took one step onto the first plank of root, and then she saw the crack. It ran across the middle of the bridge, a pale split in the braided wood, as if something enormous had pulled at it from underneath. Bits of bark had peeled away from it like old paint. Her first instinct was the one she always had. Run. Cross before you have time to be afraid. Her legs were already leaning forward, ready to do it. But the crack stared back at her, and she thought of how a root does not just break once and stay quiet about it. A root remembers. Everything that has pressed on it, every storm and every footstep, lives somewhere inside the wood. So Leyra stopped. She let out her breath, knelt at the edge where the bridge began, and laid her palm flat on the thickest root, right beside the split. The bark was rough and slightly damp. For a moment there was nothing at all, only the sound of her own heartbeat in her ears. 'I'm not here to hurry you,' she whispered. 'I only want to know where it hurts.' Then she felt it. A faint shiver came up through her hand, slow and deep, like the hum of a far-off bell. It was not words, but it was a kind of telling. The shiver gathered in the center of the bridge, where the braid was split and loose, and there it stuttered, thin and uneven, like a voice that keeps cracking. But along the edges, where the outer roots curled around the hollow like strong arms, the hum was steady and warm. Those roots were holding. They had been holding all along. Leyra drew her hand back slowly and looked at the bridge with new eyes. The middle was broken, and nothing she did right now would mend it. She was no healer of roots. But she knew now where not to step, and that felt like a small, solid treasure. She kept her hand where it was a moment longer, and in the quiet something else slid into her mind, the thing she had been trying not to think about since she arrived. The cord. She had come to the bridge hoping to cross it, yes, but also because the cord mattered, and because it was not with her. She patted her sleeve, her belt, her pockets, though she knew already what she would find. Nothing. Her hands were empty. She pressed her palm to the root again, and this time she asked the question inside her head instead of aloud. Where is the cord? A picture flickered through the wood, but it was blurry, like a face seen through rain on glass. There was a hand, she thought, and a pulling away, and the feeling of something being carried off. Leyra could have filled in the rest. It would have been so easy. A name came to the tip of her thoughts, then another, faces of people she knew, people who might have wanted the cord, or might have borrowed it. She could almost hear herself accusing one of them. But the picture had no face, and she had no right to give it one. 'I don't know who has it,' she said out loud, and the words felt strange and plain in the hollow. 'I don't know who has it, and I won't pretend I do.' The root answered with a gentle pulse, and the picture sharpened just a little, just enough. It showed her only two things. The cord was in someone else's hand. And it was not in hers. That was all. No name. No face. No place. Leyra nodded slowly. It was not much, but it was true, and a true small thing was better than a false big one. She wiped her palms on her trousers and looked across the hollow at the glowing lanterns. If the cord was in someone else's hands, then those hands belonged to someone who lived among others, someone who could be found by asking, not by guessing. The Commons was where everyone gathered. The Commons was where the oldest trees stood in a ring and listened to everything. 'Then that's where I'm going,' she said. But the bridge was still broken, and the choice of how to cross it was waiting for her. The shortest way ran straight down the middle, over the crack. It would take a few moments. It would also take a lot of luck. Leyra looked at the split, at the pale ragged edges, and shook her head. 'No,' she said quietly. 'Not that way.' She turned toward the edge instead. The outer roots curved along the rim of the hollow, longer and slower, bending out and around in a wide arc. It would take much more time to walk them. But they had hummed warm under her hand, and she trusted that hum more than she trusted her own hurry. She stepped onto the first edge root and did not put her weight on it right away. Instead she tapped it with the toe of her boot, then pressed lightly, then a little harder. It felt firm. She shifted her weight forward, and the root held, and only then did she take the next step. Tap. Press. Step. It became a rhythm, almost like a song. Below her, the hollow dropped away into green shadow, and a pale mist drifted among the lower branches. She did not look down for long. She kept her eyes on the roots in front of her and her hand brushing the lower rope-like vines that ran alongside the path. About halfway across, the bridge groaned. It was a long, low creak, and it came from the center, where the braid was split. Leyra froze. The whole bridge trembled a little, and the edge root under her boots swayed. Her heart thumped hard against her ribs. 'Easy,' she whispered, not sure whether she was talking to the bridge or to herself. 'Easy. I'm staying on the edge.' The sway settled. The edge root stayed solid beneath her. The middle kept creaking, complaining to itself, but it did not take her with it, because she was not there. She was exactly where the root had told her it was safe to be. She breathed in, breathed out, and kept going. Tap. Press. Step. She noticed which roots were thick and smooth and which were knotted and rough, which ones felt like the backs of sleeping animals and which ones felt thin and hollow, and she began to tuck those facts away in her mind like folded notes. The one with the white scar was good. The one with the twisted knot, very good. The pale one near the end, she would step over. By the time her boots touched the soft earth on the far side, her legs were shaking a little, but she was whole and dry and standing in the Commons. The bridge was still broken behind her. She had not fixed anything. But she knew its safe path by heart now, and that was a kind of gift she could carry. The Commons opened before her like a great green room. Tall old trees stood in a wide ring, their trunks gray and wrinkled, their branches meeting overhead so that the lantern light came through in soft gold patches. The ground was swept smooth by many feet, and carved benches sat between the roots. Right now it was quiet. Leyra walked to the center and looked up at the ring of trees. She did not know who might be here, or who might have been here earlier, and she did not go looking for footprints to invent a story from. She had asked herself not to guess, and she meant it. She walked to the oldest tree, the one whose bark was as deep as a river bed, and laid her hand against it. 'I came across the Root Bridge,' she said. Her voice sounded small under all those branches, but she kept going. 'It's hurt. The middle is cracked, the braid is split, and the edges are still strong. I walked the edge, and it held me. But others may not know. I don't know how to fix it by myself, and I'm asking for help. I'm not asking you to give me anything I have no right to. I'm only asking you to tell me what you remember.' For a while nothing happened. A leaf spun down and landed near her boot. Then the bark under her palm warmed, slowly, like a stone that has been sitting in the sun. The warmth traveled up her arm and spread across her shoulders, and she felt, rather than heard, a kind of answer. It was not a voice, but a gathering of old memories rising to the surface. The trees remembered the bridge. They remembered it whole, and they remembered the sound of it settling. And when she asked, carefully, about the cord, they remembered something else, something steady and sure. The cord had never moved by itself. Whenever it had changed hands, it had gone from one person to another, physically, a real passing, fingers closing around it as other fingers let go. There was no other way for it to travel. Not by wishing, not by rumor, not by accident. A hand gave, a hand received. Every time. Leyra held very still. 'So someone has it now,' she said. 'Someone who got it from someone's hand.' The warmth pulsed once, as if to agree. But when she asked who, the warmth went quiet and wide, like a lake with no wind. The trees did not know. Or they did not say. The present carrier was not in their memory, and Leyra did not push. She did not press harder on the bark or demand a name. Pulling an answer out by force would only have left her with something false. She waited, and then she stepped back and lowered her hand. 'Thank you,' she said. Her palms were empty, as before. She had no cord, no name, no direction to run. But something had changed. She had been carrying a fog of questions, who, where, why, and now the fog had a shape. She knew the question she needed to ask. It was a simple one, and it was exactly the right size: when the cord last moved, which hand gave it, and which hand took it? That was what she had to find out. She did not know the answer yet, but she knew how to ask. Leyra looked back through the trees toward the hollow, where the Root Bridge was a dark braid against the lanterns. She had a feeling in her chest, small and firm, that she was not finished with it. People would cross that bridge after her, maybe soon, maybe in a hurry like she had been. They would see the crack, or they would not. They might run for the middle. She could not leave without telling the bridge what she had learned. So she walked back, this time without hurrying and without fear, down to the edge of the hollow where the roots began. She knelt beside the same thick root she had touched at the start and pressed her palm against it. The bark felt like an old friend now. 'I'm back,' she said. 'I want to leave something with you, so you can tell whoever comes next.' She told the root everything, slowly, in plain words. She described the crack in the middle and how far it ran, and how the braid there was loose. She named the safe roots one by one, the one with the white scar, the one with the twisted knot, the long curved edge that carried her all the way across. She told it which pale root near the end to step over. She did not call herself brave. She did not say she had done anything special. She simply set down the facts the way you set down a lantern at a crossroads, so that anyone who came later would be able to see. 'The middle is dangerous,' she finished. 'Please remember it. Please tell them to go by the edge.' For a moment the root was still. Then a small shiver ran through it, short and clear, like a nod. It carried down the length of the bridge and out along the outer roots, a quick ripple of understanding. The warning had been received. Leyra let her hand rest there a moment longer. The bridge was still broken. The cord was still in somebody else's hands. Neither problem had been solved, and she did not pretend they were. But she was not lost anymore. She knew the safe way across the hollow. She knew the question she had to ask. And she knew that the trees would listen, and remember, and answer honestly when she asked them honestly. She stood up, brushed the bark dust from her knees, and looked once more at the glowing lanterns across the hollow. Then she turned toward the path that would lead her to the next person she could ask, and she walked on, ready to keep asking until the cord's whole journey, hand to hand, had been told.
